parts.problem_md:
Methylamine reacts with propanoyl chloride to form CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONHCH<sub>3</sub>.

i) State the name of the mechanism for this reaction.

[1]

An incomplete mechanism for this reaction is shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Incomplete addition-elimination mechanism diagram showing methylamine approaching propanoyl chloride with blank spaces for curly arrows, lone pairs, dipoles, and the second product](assets/001-incomplete-addition-elimination-mechanism-diagra.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

ii) Complete the mechanism in Fig. 3.1. Include all relevant curly arrows, lone pairs, and dipoles. Also show the formula of the second product formed.

[5]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the mechanism is:
> 
> - (Nucleophilic) addition-elimination **[1 mark]**

ii) The completed mechanism is:

![Completed addition-elimination mechanism showing methylamine reacting with propanoyl chloride, with all curly arrows, lone pairs, dipoles, formal charges on the intermediate, and HCl identified as the second product](assets/002-completed-addition-elimination-mechanism-showing.png)

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct dipole on the C=O bond **AND **the lone pair on the amine nitrogen
> 
> 1 mark for the curly arrow from the amine nitrogen to the δ+ carbon **AND **a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the δ– oxygen
> 
> 1 mark for the correct formal charges: – on oxygen and + on nitrogen in the intermediate **AND **the lone pair on the oxygen in the intermediate
> 
> 1 mark for the curly arrow from the N–H bond to the + nitrogen **AND **a curly arrow from the C–Cl bond to the chlorine **AND **A curly arrow from the oxygen lone pair to the C–O bond
> 
> 1 mark for HCl identified as the second product

> **[exam-tip]**
> The addition-elimination mechanism proceeds in two stages:
> 
> Addition:
> 
> - The lone pair on the nitrogen of methylamine attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon.
> - The C=O π bond breaks, the oxygen becomes negatively charged (–), and the nitrogen becomes positively charged (+).
> 
> Elimination:
> 
> - A proton is transferred from the + nitrogen to the – oxygen, then the C–Cl bond breaks as Cl– leaves, and the C=O bond reforms. HCl is produced as the second product.
> 
> Make sure you include all three curly arrows in the elimination stage: N–H to + N, C–Cl to Cl, and O lone pair to C–O.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Methylamine reacts with propanoyl chloride to form CH~3~CH~2~CONHCH~3~.

State the systematic name of the organic product formed in part **(a)**.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of the organic product is:
> 
> - *N*-methylpropanamide
> **OR**
> methylpropanamide **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When naming substituted amides:
> 
> - The acyl chloride provides the main chain:
> 
>   - propanoyl chloride → propanamide
> - The amine group is added as an N-prefix:
> 
>   - methylamine → *N*-methyl
> - Together: *N*-methylpropanamide

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Methylamine reacts with propanoyl chloride to form CH~3~CH~2~CONHCH~3~.

The organic product of part **(a)** reacts with LiAlH<sub>4</sub> to form a secondary amine.

i) State the role of LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in this reaction.

[1]

ii) State the name of the other product formed during this reaction.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The role of LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is:
> 
> - Reducing agent **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The other product formed is:
> 
> - Water **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction of *N*-methylpropanamide with LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a reduction, so the LiAlH<sub>4</sub> acts as the reducing agent.
> 
> The equation for this reduction is:
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONHCH<sub>3</sub> + 4[H] → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

parts.problem_md:
The structure of *N*-ethylethanamide is shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Structural formula of N-ethylethanamide showing an ethanoyl group connected via an NH group to an ethyl group](assets/003-structural-formula-of-n-ethylethanamide-showing-.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

i) State the reagents and conditions required to produce *N*-ethylethanamide.

[2]

ii) State the type of reaction that occurs during the formation of *N*-ethylethanamide.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions required are:
> 
> - Ethanoyl chloride / CH<sub>3</sub>COCl
> **OR**
> Ethanoic acid / CH<sub>3</sub>COOH
> **AND**
> Ethylamine / CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> / C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Room temperature (for ethanoyl chloride route)
> **OR**
> Heat under reflux (for ethanoic acid route) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The type of reaction is:
> 
> - Condensation **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Amides are formed by the condensation reaction of a carboxylic acid with an amine (producing water), or an acyl chloride with an amine (producing HCl).
> 
> To identify the reactants from the structure of an amide, break the amide (C–N) bond:
> 
> - Add –OH to the carbonyl carbon to identify the carboxylic acid (or –Cl for the acyl chloride)
> - Add –H to the nitrogen to identify the amine

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The structure of *N*-ethylethanamide is shown in Fig. 2.1.

Structural formula of N-ethylethanamide showing an ethanoyl group connected via an NH group to an ethyl group

Construct an equation to show the alkaline hydrolysis of *N*-ethylethanamide.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the alkaline hydrolysis of *N*-ethylethanamide is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CONHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + NaOH → CH<sub>3</sub>COONa + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Alkaline hydrolysis of a substituted (N-substituted) amide produces the carboxylate salt and the amine.
> 
> The amine produced retains the N-substituent. Since *N*-ethylethanamide has an ethyl group on the nitrogen, the amine product is ethylamine, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The structure of *N*-ethylethanamide is shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Structural formula of N-ethylethanamide showing an ethanoyl group connected via an NH group to an ethyl group](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/03/n-ethylethanamide.png)

State the relative order of basicity of diethylamine, *N*-ethylethanamide and ammonia in aqueous solution. Explain your reasoning.

least basic ......................... > .........................  > .........................  most basic
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The relative order of basicity (least to most basic) and explanation:
> 
> - *N*-ethylethanamide < ammonia < diethylamine **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - Alkyl groups donate electron density to the nitrogen atom, increasing the availability of the lone pair **[1 mark]**
> - The carbonyl group withdraws electron density from the nitrogen atom, reducing the availability of the lone pair **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of basicity depends on how available the nitrogen lone pair is to accept a proton:
> 
> Alkyl groups:
> 
> - Donate electron density through the inductive effect
> - Increase electron density on nitrogen, making the lone pair more available
> - Diethylamine (two ethyl groups) is a stronger base than ammonia
> 
> Carbonyl group:
> 
> - Withdraws electron density through the inductive effect
> - Decreases electron density on nitrogen, making the lone pair less available
> - *N*-ethylethanamide (carbonyl group adjacent to N) is the weakest base of the three
> 
> Be careful: exam questions sometimes swap the "least basic" and "most basic" labels. Always check which end of the table you are filling from.

parts.problem_md:
Phenylamine can be converted into the organic compounds **A** and **B** as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Reaction scheme showing two pathways from phenylamine: step 1 leads to compound A and step 2 leads to compound B, with empty boxes for student answers](assets/004-reaction-scheme-showing-two-pathways-from-phenyl.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) Draw the skeletal formulae of compounds **A** and **B** in the boxes in Fig. 1.1.

[2]

ii) State the reagents and conditions for step 1 in the box over the arrow in Fig. 1.1.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
i) The skeletal formulae of compounds **A** and **B** are:

Compound **A:**

![Skeletal formula of 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine showing a benzene ring with three bromine substituents at positions 2, 4, and 6 and an amino group](assets/005-skeletal-formula-of-2-4-6-tribromophenylamine-sh.png)

Compound **B:**

![Skeletal formula of the azo compound formed by coupling of the benzenediazonium ion, showing two benzene rings linked by an N=N group](assets/006-skeletal-formula-of-the-azo-compound-formed-by-c.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of compound **A** (2,4,6-tribromophenylamine)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of compound **B** (azo compound)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The reagents and conditions for step 1 (diazotisation) are:
> 
> - NaNO<sub>2</sub>
> **AND**
> HCl / dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
> **OR**
> HNO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Temperature ≤ 10 °C **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction of phenylamine with bromine water occurs more readily than the reaction of benzene with bromine, which requires a halogen carrier catalyst. The –NH<sub>2</sub> group activates the ring and directs bromination to positions 2, 4, and 6, giving 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine.
> 
> When phenylamine reacts with HNO<sub>2</sub> at temperatures below 10 °C, a diazonium salt is produced. Nitric(III) acid is unstable and must be freshly prepared from NaNO<sub>2</sub> and a dilute acid such as HCl. The diazonium ion then couples with a coupling agent (such as phenoxide) to form the azo compound **B**.

parts.problem_md:
When phenylamine is treated with propanoyl chloride, a white crystalline compound **C**, C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>11</sub>NO, is formed.

i) State the name of the functional group formed in this reaction.

[1]

ii) Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in **C**.

[1]

iii) Draw the structural formula of **C**.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The functional group formed is:
> 
> - Amide / secondary amide
> **OR**
> –CONHR **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in **C**:

- Calculate the molar mass of **C**:

*M*<sub>r</sub>(**C**) = (9 x 12) + (11 x 1) + 14 + 16

*M*<sub>r</sub>(**C**) = 149

- Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen:

%N = $\frac{14}{149}$ x 100

%N = **9.40%**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub> = 149 **AND** %N = 9.4(%)
> 
> A correct answer without working scores 1 mark

iii) The structural formula of **C** is:

![Structural formula of N-phenylpropanamide showing a benzene ring connected via an NH group to a propanoyl group CH2CH3CO](assets/007-structural-formula-of-n-phenylpropanamide-showin.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct structural formula of **C** (*N*-phenylpropanamide)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Phenylamine is a primary amine. When a primary amine reacts with an acyl chloride, a substituted amide is produced via an addition-elimination reaction.
> 
> The amide functional group in **C** is –CONHR (secondary amide), where R is the phenyl group from phenylamine.
> 
> To draw the structural formula of **C**, connect the nitrogen of phenylamine to the carbonyl carbon of propanoyl chloride, removing Cl from the acyl chloride and one H from the nitrogen. The result is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–NH–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.

parts.problem_md:
Fig. 1.2 shows the reduction of benzamide to form benzylamine.

![Structural formulae of benzamide and benzylamine with an arrow showing LiAlH4 reduction between them](assets/008-structural-formulae-of-benzamide-and-benzylamine.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

i) State which of these two compounds is the weaker base. Explain your answer.

[3]

ii) State the name or formula of a suitable reducing agent for this reduction.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The weaker base and explanation:
> 
> - Benzamide **[1 mark]**
> - The carbonyl / C=O group is electron-withdrawing **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair on the nitrogen atom is less available to donate / less available to accept a proton **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A suitable reducing agent is:
> 
> - LiAlH<sub>4</sub> / lithium aluminium hydride **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzamide is a weaker base than benzylamine because the carbonyl group (C=O) adjacent to the nitrogen is electron-withdrawing. This reduces the electron density on the nitrogen atom, making the lone pair less available to accept a proton.
> 
> Both compounds contain the electron-withdrawing benzene ring, but this affects both equally. The key difference is the C=O group in benzamide, which is absent in benzylamine.
> 
> LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is required for the reduction of amides to amines. NaBH<sub>4</sub> is not strong enough to reduce the C=O group in an amide.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.2 shows the reduction of benzamide to form benzylamine.

When benzamide is refluxed with dilute acid, hydrolysis occurs.

i) Draw the skeletal formula of the organic product formed.

[1]

ii) State the name of the other product formed during this hydrolysis reaction.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) The skeletal formula of the organic product is:

![Skeletal formula of benzoic acid showing a benzene ring with a COOH group](assets/009-skeletal-formula-of-benzoic-acid-showing-a-benze.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of benzoic acid
> 
> ii) The other product formed is:
> 
> - Ammonium ion / NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> / ammonium salt **[1 mark]**
> -

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a non-substituted amide is hydrolysed with dilute acid, the nitrogen leaves as ammonium ion (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>), not free ammonia. The organic product is the carboxylic acid (benzoic acid).
> 
> For alkaline hydrolysis, the products would instead be the carboxylate salt (sodium benzoate) and ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>).
> 
> ![Displayed formula showing the acid hydrolysis of benzamide to form benzoic acid and ammonium ions](assets/010-displayed-formula-showing-the-acid-hydrolysis-of.png)

parts.problem_md:
Amides can be formed from amines. An example is shown in the following reaction scheme where compound **X** reacts with methylamine to form *N*-methylpropanamide and hydrogen chloride.

compound **X** + CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONHCH<sub>3</sub> + HCl

Deduce the structural formula of compound **X**.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The structural formula of compound **X** is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Amides are formed by the reaction of an amine with an acyl chloride. In this case, the primary amine CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> reacts with propanoyl chloride, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl, to form the substituted amide and hydrochloric acid.

parts.problem_md: *N*-methylpropanamide can undergo reduction forming compound **Y** and water. State the reagent required for this reaction.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagent required for this reduction is:
> 
> - LiAlH<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> *N*-methylpropanamide is a substituted amide. When reduced with LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, it forms a secondary amine (compound **Y**) and water.
> 
> LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a strong enough reducing agent for this reaction. NaBH<sub>4</sub> is not strong enough to reduce amides.

parts.problem_md:
A different amide, ethanamide, was heated with sodium hydroxide; ammonia gas is formed along with one other product.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Explain how this reaction could be used as a test for an amide.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> + NaOH → CH<sub>3</sub>COONa + NH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) This reaction can be used as a test for an amide by:
> 
> - Hold damp red litmus paper above the heated reaction mixture **[1 mark]**
> - The paper turns blue **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When ethanamide is heated with sodium hydroxide solution, ammonia gas is produced and sodium ethanoate remains in solution.
> 
> Ammonia is an alkaline gas, so it turns damp red litmus paper blue. This test confirms the presence of the amide functional group, which undergoes alkaline hydrolysis to release NH<sub>3</sub>.
